Nine Gold Medals

a poem by David Roth

Nine athletes. One hundred yards. One fall — and a finish the crowd never forgot. Step through the poem stanza by stanza, touch the difficult words, and test yourself the way your textbook does.

9 athletes 8 stanzas 1 finish line 0 losers
Play the poem Read it stanza by stanza

The poem, as a film

Press play and let it unfold

Eight scenes, one race. The pictures drift as the poem comes up a line at a time — watch it straight through, or step scene by scene.

The athletes had come from all over the country

To run for the gold, for the silver and bronze

Many weeks and months of training

All coming down to these games.

The spectators gathered around the old field

To cheer on all the young women and men

The final event of the day was approaching

Excitement was high to begin.

The blocks were all lined up for those who would use them

The hundred-yard dash and the race to be run

These were nine resolved athletes in the back of the starting line

Poised for the sound of the gun.

The signal was given, the pistol exploded

And so did the runners all charging ahead

But the smallest among them, he stumbled and staggered

And fell to the asphalt instead.

He gave out a cry of frustration and anguish

His dreams and his efforts dashed in the dirt

But as sure as I’m standing here telling this story

The same goes for what next occurred.

The eight other runners pulled up on their heels

The ones who had trained for so long to compete

One by one they all turned round and went back to help him

And brought the young boy to his feet.

Then all the nine runners joined hands and continued

The hundred-yard dash now reduced to a walk

And a banner above that said (Special Olympics)

Could not have been more on the mark.

That’s how the race ended, with nine gold medals

They came to the finish line holding hands still

And a standing ovation and nine beaming faces

Said more than these words ever will.

Nine gold medals — and not one of them

crossed that line alone.

Before the gun goes off

Which games are these?

The poem unfolds at a Special Olympics meet. Before you read, get the three great games straight — the exercise your textbook calls Reflect and Respond.

Official symbol
The oldest games · since 776 BC

The Olympics

Born at Olympia in ancient Greece as a festival of Zeus, the modern Games gather athletes of every nation every four years, summer and winter. The five rings stand for the five continents meeting in friendship.

Motto: Citius, Altius, Fortius, Communiter — Faster, Higher, Stronger, Together.
Official symbol — the Agitos
Agitos — “I move”

The Paralympics

A parallel stage for athletes with physical, visual and other disabilities, held alongside the Olympic Games. Its symbol, the three Agitos, comes from the Latin for “I move”.

Para athletes compete in classifications so that ability, not disability, decides the medal.
Official emblem
The stage of this poem

The Special Olympics

Year-round sports training and athletic competition for children and adults with intellectual disabilities. It strives to create a better world by fostering the acceptance and inclusion of all people.

Here, the race in stanza 7 runs under a banner that says exactly that.

Reflect & respond

Empathy, sympathy, compassion — can you tell them apart?

Each voice below means well. Tap the word each sentence shows, then check yourself.

Voice A
“I am so sorry for what is happening to you. It is sad — do you want something to eat?”
Voice B
“I can imagine how you feel. I understand why you are feeling terribly low.”
Voice C
“I understand why you are upset. I will spend some time with you, so that you don’t feel lonely.”
Pick a word for each voice first.

The race, stanza by stanza

Walk the hundred yards with them

Eight stanzas, eight plates. Move through the race with the arrows or your keyboard, and tap any dotted word for its meaning.

Stanza 01 · The gathering

From every corner of the country

The athletes had come from all over the country
To run for the gold, for the silver and bronze
Many weeks and months of training
All coming down to these games.

What happens hereThe poem opens wide: athletes from across the country, months of sweat, everything riding on one day of games — gold, silver or bronze at stake.
SettingVisual imagery
Stanza 02 · The crowd

The old field fills up

The spectators gathered around the old field
To cheer on all the young women and men
The final event of the day was approaching
Excitement was high to begin.

What happens hereThe crowd circles a humble, worn ground — not a grand stadium — as the day’s final event approaches. Men and women are cheered alike, and expectation hangs in the air.
AtmosphereAnticipation
Stanza 03 · The start

Nine, poised at the blocks

The blocks were all lined up for those who would use them
The hundred-yard dash and the race to be run
These were nine resolved athletes in the back of the starting line
Poised for the sound of the gun.

What happens hereNine determined athletes crouch at the starting line of the hundred-yard dash. The stanza slows time down to a single held breath — everyone waiting for the pistol.
TensionForeshadowing
Stanza 04 · The turning point

The gun, the burst, the fall

The signal was given, the pistol exploded
And so did the runners all charging ahead
But the smallest among them, he stumbled and staggered
And fell to the asphalt instead.

What happens hereThe race explodes off the line — and in a single line the poem turns. The smallest runner stumbles, staggers, and hits the track instead of finishing the charge.
Turning pointAlliterationContrast
Stanza 05 · The low point

A cry in the dirt

He gave out a cry of frustration and anguish
His dreams and his efforts dashed in the dirt
But as sure as I’m standing here telling this story
The same goes for what next occurred.

What happens hereThe boy’s cry carries his months of effort collapsing at once — dreams “dashed in the dirt”. The poet leans in like a storyteller: but as sure as I’m standing here… something extraordinary follows.
Auditory imageryIdiomStoryteller’s aside
Stanza 06 · The reversal

Eight turn around

The eight other runners pulled up on their heels
The ones who had trained for so long to compete
One by one they all turned round and went back to help him
And brought the young boy to his feet.

What happens hereEight athletes abandon their own race — months of training set aside in a heartbeat — and turn back, one by one, to lift the fallen boy. Empathy defeats competition.
Empathy in actionReversal
Stanza 07 · The walk

Nine hands, one banner

Then all the nine runners joined hands and continued
The hundred-yard dash now reduced to a walk
And a banner above that said (Special Olympics)
Could not have been more on the mark.

What happens hereThe sprint becomes a walk, nine hands joined — and the banner overhead, Special Olympics, turns out to be more prophecy than label: acceptance and inclusion, exactly as the movement intends.
SymbolismIrony of the banner
Stanza 08 · The finish

Nine gold medals

That’s how the race ended, with nine gold medals
They came to the finish line holding hands still
And a standing ovation and nine beaming faces
Said more than these words ever will.

What happens hereAll nine cross together, hands still joined, to a standing ovation. Nine golds — because on this day, kindness was the event. The closing line admits that some moments outgrow words entirely.
ResolutionMessage

The chapter in pictures

From page to picture

The scenes that carry the poem, together with the original artwork printed in the Kaveri textbook.

Poetic devices used in the poem

Each device, with its example from the poem.

Alliteration
Repeating the same sound at the start of nearby words: “he stumbled and staggered” and “his dreams and his efforts dashed in the dirt”.
Visual imagery
Words that paint a picture: “nine resolved athletes … poised for the sound of the gun”, “holding hands still” at the finish, and “nine beaming faces”.
Auditory imagery
Words that let us hear the moment: “the pistol exploded” and the boy’s “cry of frustration and anguish”.
Symbolism
The joined hands stand for solidarity, the Special Olympics banner for inclusion, and the dash “reduced to a walk” for winning that no longer matters.
Tone & mood
The tone moves from excitement to anguish to quiet triumph; the mood it leaves is warm and uplifting.
Message
Empathy is the highest form of victory — helping a fallen friend matters more than finishing first.

Learning beyond the text

Where the story keeps running

The Special Olympic Games 2023 were held in Berlin, Germany — and Indian athletes came home shining.

400 m · Level C · Women

Ravimathi Arumugam

Made India proud by clinching the gold medal in the 400-metre, Level C women’s race.

400 m · Level B · Women

Aanchal Goyal

Won the gold medal in the 400-metre, Level B women’s race.

Mini javelin & 400 m · Level B · Men

Saket Kundu

Achieved a rare double in track and field — silver in the Level B mini javelin, bronze in the Level B 400-metre race.

776 BC

The first Olympic Games

The original Olympics began as part of an ancient Greek festival celebrating Zeus, the god of sky and weather.

Every four years

Faster, Higher, Stronger — Together

The Olympic motto Citius-Altius-Fortius-Communiter translates to “Faster-Higher-Stronger-Together”, alternating between summer and winter editions.

1913

The five rings

Designed to include everyone — the rings represent the union of the five continents and the meeting of athletes from throughout the world.

Before every Games

The torch

A flame is lit at Olympia, Greece — a symbol of peace and friendship — and carried over several weeks to the host city, where the cauldron opens the Games.

Paralympics

The Agitos — “I move”

The Paralympics showcase para-athletes with disabilities across sports; its symbol, the Agitos, is the visual voice of the Paralympic Movement.

Special Olympics

A better world, together

Sports training and athletic competition for children and adults with intellectual disabilities — fostering the acceptance and inclusion of all people.

Berlin, 2023

India’s golden run

Ravimathi Arumugam and Aanchal Goyal strike gold; Saket Kundu lands a silver and a bronze — the poem’s spirit, alive on a real track.

The Poet

David Roth

David Roth is an American singer-songwriter and storyteller whose songs carry the same qualities this poem does — warmth, plain words, and a turn that catches you unprepared. Nine Gold Medals has the cadence of a song because it was written to be sung; classrooms now read it as a poem.

The folk legend Tom Paxton called Nine Gold Medals “one of the best songs I’ve heard in the last 20 years”. The poem retells a race run at a Special Olympics meet, where the field did something the rulebook never imagined: it stopped, turned around, and finished together.
